title: Grid Ramsey Problem (gr(G_{2x2}, K_n))
statement_text: What is the minimum $N$ such that any 2-edge-coloring of the Cartesian product $K_N \square K_N$ contains either a red rectangle or a blue $K_n$?
context_text: The $N\times N$ grid graph $G_{N\times N}=K_N\square K_N$ has vertex set $[N]\times[N]$, two vertices being adjacent when they share exactly one coordinate; a rectangle is a $2\times2$ subgrid, i.e. four vertices $(x,y),(x,y'),(x',y'),(x',y)$ with the four axis-parallel edges between them. $\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every $2$-edge-colouring of $G_{N\times N}$ contains a red rectangle or a blue $K_n$ (a clique of $G_{N\times N}$ lies in a single row or column). Via the bipartite $3$-graph $B^{(3)}(N,N)$ on $[2N]$ (all triples meeting both halves), whose triples correspond to the edges of the grid, rectangles correspond to copies of $K_4^{(3)}$ and $n$-cliques to copies of $S_n^{(3)}$; hence $\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every $2$-colouring of $B^{(3)}(N,N)$ has a red $K_4^{(3)}$ or a blue $S_n^{(3)}$, and $r(K_4^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})\le2\,\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)$. The authors introduce this grid Ramsey problem as the key tool for estimating $r(K_4^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})$, and prove $2^{c\log^2n}\le\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)\le2^{c'n^{2/3}\log n}$ for positive constants $c,c'$; the exact growth rate remains open. They note a curious similarity with the lower bound $2^{c(\log r)^{2.5}/\sqrt{\log\log r}}$ for the grid case of Shelah's cube lemma ($r$ colours), without finding any connection.

title: Informal Conjecture: r(K^(3)_4, S^(3)_n) and gr(G_{2x2}, K_n) have the same order
statement_text: We strongly believe that $r(K^{(3)}_4, S^{(3)}_n)$ and $\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times 2}, K_n)$ are of roughly the same order.
context_text: A $3$-graph is a $3$-uniform hypergraph; $K_s^{(3)}$ is the complete $3$-graph on $s$ vertices, $K_4^{(3)}-e$ is $K_4^{(3)}$ minus one edge (three triples on four vertices), and the star $3$-graph $S_n^{(3)}$ has $n+1$ vertices and all $\binom{n}{2}$ triples containing a given vertex. The Ramsey number $r(H_1,H_2)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every $3$-graph on $N$ vertices contains $H_1$ or its complement contains $H_2$ (equivalently, every red/blue colouring of the triples of $K_N^{(3)}$ has a red $H_1$ or a blue $H_2$). The $N\times N$ grid graph $G_{N\times N}=K_N\square K_N$ has vertex set $[N]\times[N]$, two vertices being adjacent when they share exactly one coordinate; a rectangle is a $2\times2$ subgrid, i.e. four vertices $(x,y),(x,y'),(x',y'),(x',y)$ with the four axis-parallel edges between them. $\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every $2$-edge-colouring of $G_{N\times N}$ contains a red rectangle or a blue $K_n$ (a clique of $G_{N\times N}$ lies in a single row or column). Rectangles in $G_{N\times N}$ correspond to copies of $K_4^{(3)}$ and $n$-cliques to copies of $S_n^{(3)}$ in the bipartite $3$-graph $B^{(3)}(N,N)\subseteq K_{2N}^{(3)}$, which gives $r(K_4^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})\le2\,\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)$. No direct implication between the lower bounds is known, but the authors glue together copies of their lower-bound construction for $\mathrm{gr}(G_{2\times2},K_n)$ to obtain one for $r(K_4^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})$ of comparable size; both quantities satisfy $2^{c\log^2n}\le\cdot\le2^{c'n^{2/3}\log n}$. This intermediate growth (between polynomial and exponential) contrasts with $r(K_s^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})=2^{\Theta(n)}$ for $s\ge5$ and with the Erdős–Hajnal polynomial-to-exponential transition phenomenon for Ramsey numbers against cliques.

title: Informal Conjecture: r(K^(3)_{4-e}, S^(3)_n) = Theta(n^2 / log n)
statement_text: The close connection between $r(K_4^{(3)}-e, S^{(3)}_n)$ and $r(K_3, K_n)$ suggests that $r(K_4^{(3)}-e, S^{(3)}_n) = \Theta\!\left(\frac{n^2}{\log n}\right)$.
context_text: A $3$-graph is a $3$-uniform hypergraph; $K_s^{(3)}$ is the complete $3$-graph on $s$ vertices, $K_4^{(3)}-e$ is $K_4^{(3)}$ minus one edge (three triples on four vertices), and the star $3$-graph $S_n^{(3)}$ has $n+1$ vertices and all $\binom{n}{2}$ triples containing a given vertex. The Ramsey number $r(H_1,H_2)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every $3$-graph on $N$ vertices contains $H_1$ or its complement contains $H_2$ (equivalently, every red/blue colouring of the triples of $K_N^{(3)}$ has a red $H_1$ or a blue $H_2$). The paper studies $r(K_s^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})$ for fixed $s$ and growing $n$, the regime left open by Fox and He. By the Lovász Local Lemma the authors obtain $c\frac{n^2}{\log^2n}\le r(K_4^{(3)}-e,S_n^{(3)})\le c'\frac{n^2}{\log n}$, which parallels the graph Ramsey number $r(K_3,K_n)=\Theta(n^2/\log n)$. They believe that the upper bound is the truth and that a proof may be possible through a careful analysis of the $(K_4^{(3)}-e)$-free process, but do not pursue this. For comparison, they show $2^{c\log^2n}\le r(K_4^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})\le2^{c'n^{2/3}\log n}$ and $r(K_s^{(3)},S_n^{(3)})=2^{\Theta(n)}$ for $s\ge5$.
